entry.title: Qwen.ai launches Qwen4-Max, a new AI model announced in November 2026
entry.summary: Qwen.ai has introduced Qwen4-Max, a new AI model detailed in a blog post published in November 2026. The announcement has generated discussion and interest within the AI community, as reflected in related Hacker News threads.

entry.title: Job postings on Hacker News remain near 12-year lows in November 2026 as AI skills appear in over half of listings [ * ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Job postings on the Hacker News "Who is Hiring?" thread have stayed near their lowest levels since 2014, with November 2026 showing a 37% drop from the previous year and an average of 287 postings per month for the year, the lowest since 2013. Meanwhile, AI-related skills are now mentioned in 51.6% of postings, up from 30% two years ago, reflecting a shift in demand toward AI agents and related technologies. The data also shows a decline in front-end roles from 27% of postings in early 2022 to 6.6% in November 2026, with full-stack and back-end roles also decreasing. Python and TypeScript remain the top programming languages, though Rust has risen to third place. Remote work continues to dominate, appearing in 55.7% of postings, with onsite and hybrid arrangements relatively stable. The analysis includes new AI-related terms and corrections to previous data to provide a comprehensive view of hiring trends.

entry.title: Researchers analyze 516 multi-agent LLM configurations, finding multi-agent accuracy often matches or falls below single-pass baselines when controlling for sample count and compute [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers conducted a comprehensive evaluation of multi-agent language models, synthesizing nine empirical studies with 516 unique configurations to disentangle the effects of coordination, sample multiplicity, and inference compute. They found that multi-agent systems generally do not outperform single-pass baselines when matched for sample count or resource budget, with accuracy differences averaging slightly negative and multi-agent accuracy equaling or falling below baselines in 74% of comparable cases. The study highlights that communication among agents only improves performance when evidence is partitioned, externally verified, or models exhibit diverse errors, and provides tools for reviewers to assess such systems.

entry.title: Researchers introduce WebArena-Pro, a reproducible benchmark with 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications supporting multimodal inputs including audio and video [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: WebArena-Pro is a new benchmark designed to evaluate web agents powered by large language and vision-language models across diverse applications and multimodal content. It includes 300 tasks spanning 20 self-hosted web applications in six domains, supporting text, vision, audio, and video modalities with reproducible, parallel evaluation. The benchmark aims to address limitations of existing benchmarks that cover fewer applications, restrict modalities, or sacrifice reproducibility due to live site changes. The benchmark features tasks authored through a dedicated interface, filtered by large language model-assisted triage, and validated by humans. Evaluations show that Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 achieve the highest performance at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.7%. WebArena-Pro provides the broadest application coverage and most comprehensive multimodal support among reproducible, human-curated web agent benchmarks to date.

entry.title: ModHarness-RL introduces learnable, evolving harness programs for agentic reinforcement learning to improve model context and guidance during training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: ModHarness-RL recasts the harness in agentic reinforcement learning as programs that are learned from data and evolve alongside the model during training. It uses structured state representations and two core program components-a Compression program to assemble interaction history and a Steering program to guide behavior deviations. This approach was tested on CodeSearch, ALFWorld, and BIRD SQL with models ranging from 1.5B to 8B parameters, showing improved held-out performance compared to fixed harness baselines in most cases. The system proposes candidate harness programs from recent trajectories, verifies them through execution, and replays them over past trajectories to adapt to shifts in model behavior. These results suggest that harnesses can be dynamically learned and evolved from task data, potentially enhancing agentic RL performance across domains and models.

entry.title: Researchers propose Self-Disagreement training to improve language models' dialectical competence without external opposition or human annotation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a method called Self-Disagreement to train language models in dialectical competence-the ability to know when to hold or yield a position-by generating and evaluating their own counterarguments without relying on external models or human feedback. This approach uses reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards based on the same checks that score answers, enabling models to improve this capability independently of first-answer accuracy. The method involves the model stating a position, creating the strongest opposing case, ruling on its validity, and training on that ruling, all within a single model during training and deployment. This capability emerges through training rather than being elicited, allowing models to resist challenges from stronger opponents they were never explicitly trained against. The findings suggest that the necessary opposition for improvement can come from the model itself rather than external sources.

entry.title: Researchers use activation steering to control narrative flow in AI-generated adaptation of Joseph Conrad's Typhoon [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers created an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella Typhoon, using a large language model seeded with the original text to generate continuous output that evolves over time. They applied activation steering techniques, including a novel adaptive method, to manage the narrative rhythm and the model's digressions during extended generation. This project explores the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI systems and their inherent unpredictability and complexity beyond human control.

entry.title: LuthorSQL launches a 7B parameter non-autoregressive text-to-SQL model to reduce API costs by 33% by serving as a fast System 1 filter for slower LLM agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: LuthorSQL is a 7B parameter non-autoregressive text-to-SQL model designed to act as a rapid System 1 gate for slower large language model (LLM) agents, escalating queries only when uncertain. It achieves 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set with an average latency of 0.84 seconds per query on a single GPU and maintains accuracy with 8-bit quantization. The model transfers zero-shot to multiple SQL databases with minimal accuracy loss compared to SQLite. When combined with the Claude Opus 5.5 agent in a confidence cascade, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all queries locally, reducing API costs by one-third without sacrificing accuracy. Additional analysis shows that Opus reproduces a large portion of public benchmark queries verbatim but maintains high tool-assisted accuracy on renamed schemas and databases published after its training cutoff. The code and data for LuthorSQL are publicly available.

entry.title: Researchers develop interactive program induction algorithm using language model priors that selects informative queries to recover target programs with fewer examples [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a Bayesian approach to program induction where a learner recovers a target program from limited input-output examples by interactively selecting maximally informative inputs and querying an oracle for outputs. The method uses a language model as a prior and a greedy query-selection algorithm that terminates after a bounded number of queries, returning the target program up to approximate equivalence under certain conditions. The algorithm applies a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence and estimates the query-selection objective via importance sampling. Evaluated on the CodeARC benchmark, it improves accuracy by up to 22 percentage points compared to a language model-only agent while requiring up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples, demonstrating more efficient program induction through interactive querying.

entry.title: Researchers introduce UMPIRE, a training-free uncertainty quantification framework for multimodal large language models that uses incoherence-adjusted semantic volume to improve error detection and calibration across various modalities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed UMPIRE, a new framework for quantifying uncertainty in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that operates without additional training or external tools. UMPIRE calculates an incoherence-adjusted semantic volume based on the models' internal features, capturing both semantic diversity and response incoherence to better identify errors and calibrate uncertainty across text, image, audio, and video tasks. UMPIRE is inspired by Determinantal Point Processes and combines semantic embedding dispersion with quadratic entropy to assess model confidence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UMPIRE outperforms existing uncertainty metrics on multiple benchmarks, even with limited sample sizes, and generalizes to non-text outputs such as image and audio generation. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further use and evaluation.

entry.title: Researchers present LEGAL-UQA, a parallel English-Urdu benchmark of 619 constitutional question-answer pairs for testing legal QA systems for Urdu speakers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: LEGAL-UQA provides a dataset linking questions, reference answers, and source passages from Pakistan's Constitution in both English and Urdu to support development of legal information assistants for Urdu speakers. The study evaluates two tasks separately: answering Urdu questions given source passages and retrieving relevant passages for each question. It also compares an automated decision model, JEV, with human grading, finding that retrieval methods based on simple word matching outperform embedding methods and that JEV agrees with human grades less often than a baseline giving full credit to all answers. The research highlights the importance of separate testing for retrieval and answering, inclusion of simple retrieval baselines, and human validation of automated judges and reference answers when building legal QA software for Urdu speakers.

entry.title: ROCKET introduces a training-free model compression method using knapsack optimization and sparse matrix factorization, achieving over 90% performance retention at 30% compression without fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: ROCKET is a model compression technique that operates without training, optimizing layer-wise compression as a multi-choice knapsack problem to minimize reconstruction error under a global size constraint. It uses a single-step sparse matrix factorization inspired by dictionary learning, leveraging a small calibration set to sparsify weights based on activation sensitivity and updating the dictionary via least squares without iterative optimization or backpropagation. The method consistently outperforms existing compression approaches across various architectures at 20-50% compression rates, retaining over 90% of original model performance at 30% compression without fine-tuning. With light fine-tuning, ROCKET further improves recovery, demonstrated by compressing Qwen3-14B to an 8B-parameter model and achieving performance close to the original Qwen3-8B after training on 30 million tokens. The ROCKET code is publicly available on GitHub.

entry.title: FlashSampling fuses exact sampling into LM-head matmul to reduce memory use and speed up large-vocabulary decoding on datacenter GPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: FlashSampling is a new exact sampling method that integrates sampling directly into the language model head matrix multiplication, avoiding the need to materialize the full logits tensor in high-bandwidth memory. It computes logits tile-by-tile on-chip, adds Gumbel noise, and performs a reduction to select samples efficiently. The approach replaces all-gather communication with streaming peer-to-peer writes in tensor-parallel decoding, enabling near-ideal scaling across up to eight GPUs. FlashSampling achieves kernel-level speedups on multiple datacenter GPUs including H100, H200, B200, and B300, and reduces time per output token by up to 10% in end-to-end vLLM experiments. These results demonstrate that exact sampling without approximation can be efficiently incorporated into the matmul operation, consolidating bandwidth-bound sampling steps and improving decoding performance.

entry.title: Researchers release TransitLM, a large-scale dataset of 13 million transit route records from four Chinese cities for map-free transit route generation using large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have introduced TransitLM, a dataset containing nearly 13 million public transit route planning records from four Chinese cities, covering over 120,000 stations and 13,600 lines. The dataset supports training large language models (LLMs) to generate transit routes without relying on structured maps or routing engines, enabling end-to-end route planning directly from origin-destination data. Experiments with LLMs trained on TransitLM show high accuracy in producing structurally valid routes and the ability to implicitly associate GPS coordinates with appropriate stations without explicit mapping. The dataset and benchmark include three evaluation tasks with complementary metrics and are publicly available along with evaluation code.

entry.title: Researchers introduce QVal, a training-free testbed to evaluate dense supervision signals for long-horizon LLM agents by measuring Q-alignment across multiple methods and environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present QVal, a testbed designed to evaluate dense supervision signals for large language model (LLM) agents acting over long horizons by measuring how well these signals align with the expected returns of candidate actions without requiring full training. They benchmarked 21 methods from seven families using six open-weight backbones across four environments, finding that simple prompting baselines generally achieve the highest Q-alignment, while other methods vary in effectiveness depending on the environment and action space size. The study reveals that code-generated signals perform well only in small state and action spaces, embedding-based signals are weak, self-distillation signals are often anti-aligned, and no method achieves Q-alignment in open-ended environments. Additionally, when these signals guide an actor in selecting actions at test time, higher Q-alignment correlates strongly with improved task success. QVal is designed to be extensible, allowing researchers to compare new dense supervision signals efficiently before committing to full training runs.

entry.title: URSA introduces a chemistry-aware benchmark for evaluating retrosynthesis planning, comparing deep-learning systems and large language models on novel drug discovery tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: URSA (Utilitarian RetroSynthesis Assessment) is a new evaluation framework designed to benchmark synthetic routes for target molecules by assessing both formal criteria, such as availability of starting materials, and chemical plausibility, reflecting expert chemists' evaluations. The study applies URSA to compare conventional end-to-end retrosynthesis tools and large language models (LLMs) on diverse, novel molecules with undisclosed synthetic routes, representing realistic drug design challenges. While LLMs demonstrate strong strategic planning and achieve state-of-the-art performance on out-of-distribution sets, the most cost-effective and chemically plausible routes are produced exclusively by specialized retrosynthesis planners.

entry.title: Researchers analyze unembedding matrix dynamics in language model pretraining, revealing early encoding of task information before readout expression in Pythia model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied when language models acquire capabilities by examining the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is learned during pretraining and affects output expression. They introduced parameter-trajectory crosscoding to track readout changes directly, finding that Pythia's readout reorganizes early in training, making WordNet word categories decodable before the model's outputs reflect this information. Experiments varying the readout learning rate showed that faster readout learning closes the gap between encoded and expressed information without impacting final loss. These findings suggest that behavioral milestones in early training may reflect when the readout expresses task knowledge rather than when the model itself learns it.

entry.title: Researchers introduce NaijaFacts benchmark to separate language proficiency from factual knowledge in AI models across Nigerian languages and compare with US/UK data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed NaijaFacts, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria in English, Nigerian Pidgin, Yorùbá, Igbo, and Hausa, to evaluate AI models' knowledge versus language ability. Testing across eight models showed that knowledge gaps dominate performance issues, with accuracy around 20% for Nigerian facts compared to 49-50% for US/UK facts in English queries. Language effects were smaller and correlated with web representation of languages. The strongest models scored up to 79% on UK/US data but did not exceed 31% on Nigerian statistics. Extending the evaluation to all 54 African countries revealed similar patterns, indicating a continent-wide knowledge gap rather than a Nigeria-specific issue.

entry.title: Researchers introduce JudgeMix, a judge-guided data synthesis framework that dynamically combines expert and target model guidance to improve LLM agent training, showing up to 10 pass@1 point gains on tool-use benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: JudgeMix addresses the training-inference distribution mismatch in supervised fine-tuning of large language model (LLM) agents by selectively querying expert guidance only when the target model struggles, based on step-wise semantic evaluations. This approach preserves the model's correct behaviors while correcting errors, maintaining alignment with the target model's state distribution. Evaluated on two agentic tool-use benchmarks, AppWorld and AutomationBench, JudgeMix consistently outperforms existing methods with significant improvements in success rates.

entry.title: Researchers define natural-language-rooted depth to measure opaque serial cognition in AI models, correlating with layer count and suggesting new architecture impacts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A recent study introduces natural-language-rooted (NLS) depth as a measure of opaque serial cognition in AI models, representing the longest computational path without passing through interpretable bottlenecks. This measure is determined by architecture and training configurations before model training and correlates strongly with model layer count, having increased gradually over recent years. The research indicates that standard transformer scaling may only slowly increase NLS depth, while alternative architectures like full-bandwidth transformers could significantly enhance it. The authors recommend that AI developers track and report NLS depth alongside chain-of-thought monitorability to better understand model interpretability.

entry.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A recent study explored how different framing effects influence the behavior of a large language model (LLM) agent in a simulated market environment based on real litigation transcripts. Using the Gemma 3 12B model, researchers tested how gain, loss, blame, and credit frames affected the agent's willingness to engage in collusive behavior related to silver pricing. Results showed that loss and blame frames increased collusion rates, while management pressure increased trading volume but not collusion. Further experiments injecting internal states corresponding to these frames revealed that loss and blame states made the agent more cautious, whereas gain and credit states increased collusion tendencies. These findings highlight the impact of psychological framing on AI decision-making in economic simulations.

entry.title: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A new training method called Model Annealing has been introduced to improve data-efficient learning by incorporating review and consolidation phases during training. The approach divides training into episodes with cyclical learning rates and leverages a memory of past model states to guide learning, including generating adversarial examples where the current model and memory disagree. Evaluated on datasets like CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet across various architectures, Model Annealing generally improves accuracy, calibration, and robustness compared to standard cross-entropy training and snapshot distillation, particularly with AdamW optimizers. While it may reduce accuracy for some models like SGD-trained ResNet-18, it still enhances robustness to adversarial perturbations. The method addresses issues of overconfidence and fitting degradation through its memory and adversarial components.

entry.title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

entry.title: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.

entry.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.

entry.title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.

entry.title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.

entry.title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

entry.title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(http://cai.1688.com/), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.

entry.title: Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.

entry.title: LACCO: Local Accumulation with Computation--Communication Overlap [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training language models across low-bandwidth networks requires reducing synchronization overhead. Local optimization methods such as DiLoCo communicate only after several local steps, but outer gradient averaging and the outer update remain on the critical path. Existing computation-communication overlap methods avoid this stall through delayed or replica-local updates, which can degrade convergence or cause replicas to drift. We propose LACCO (Local Accumulation with Computation-Communication Overlap), a two-stage algorithm that overlaps global communication with local computation while applying globally aggregated updates shared by every replica, without introducing staleness in the outer update. We establish convergence guarantees for smooth non-convex objectives. Experiments on language-model pre-training with FineWeb show that LACCO consistently outperforms communication-overlapped baselines such as Eager and Delayed DiLoCo. These gains remain robust as model size scales up to 0.5B parameters and across a range of communication intervals and numbers of replicas up to 16 workers, while incurring only negligible-or fully overlappable-computational or memory overhead, which demonstrates the strength of LACCO.

entry.title: When evaluation becomes intervention in clinical AI [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18297v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI judges, models that grade another system's output against a rubric, extend clinical review to the scale at which clinical AI writes. When teams use judge assessments to select a prompt or train a model, the judge becomes part of the intervention. Selection can then favor errors the judge overlooks. We describe what a judge's report must contain and the independent clinical test each judge-driven change needs.

entry.title: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.

entry.title: HARDTESTGEN: A High-Quality RL Verifier Generation Pipeline for LLM Algorithmic Coding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2505.24098v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Verifiers provide important reward signals for reinforcement learning of large language models (LLMs). However, it is challenging to develop or create reliable verifiers, especially for code generation tasks. A well-disguised wrong solution program may only be detected by carefully human-written edge cases that are difficult to synthesize automatically. To address this issue, we propose HARDTESTGEN, an approach to synthesize high-quality test cases for algorithmic coding problems. We curate a comprehensive algorithmic programming dataset HARDTESTS with 26.6k problems and high-quality synthetic tests. Compared with existing tests, HARDTESTGEN tests demonstrate significantly higher accuracy in verifying LLM-generated code (+11.22 percentage points in precision, the percentage of actually correct code within the predicted correct ones). We also show that downstream post-training -- including rejection sampling and reinforcement learning (RL) -- using HARDTESTS verifier results in improved performance of LLM code generation. We open-source our dataset and synthesis pipeline at https://leililab.github.io/HardTests/.

entry.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Sequence Models for Sample-Efficient Energy Regression in Simulated Calorimeter Showers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17354v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Energy reconstruction from electromagnetic calorimeter data underpins particle identification, event reconstruction and precision measurements in high-energy physics. Machine learning already performs well on this task, yet two questions remain open: how much the choice of data representation matters, and whether hybrid quantum-classical models add value in practice. We compare classical and quantum-enhanced models for incident positron energy reconstruction on the CaloGAN dataset, a public benchmark of 100,000 simulated electromagnetic shower events spanning 1 to 100 GeV. Eight architectures, namely SVR, ANN, CNN and LSTM together with their quantum counterparts, are trained on three calorimeter representations: engineered physical features, calorimeter images, and longitudinal shower sequences. Models that follow the longitudinal development of the shower reach the highest accuracy, which points to the value of physically informed representations. The hybrid QLSTM gives the lowest reconstruction error, with an RMSE of 0.294 GeV. Under matched-data conditions with only 1,500 training events, the QLSTM improves on the classical LSTM by 52.7% and also surpasses an LSTM trained on the full set. These observations indicate that longitudinal representations are central to calorimeter energy reconstruction and give preliminary evidence that hybrid quantum-classical sequence models can be more sample-efficient for regression in high-energy physics.

entry.title: Enumerating Posterior-Supported Priors: First-Order Error of Finite-Integral Cross-Categorical Measurement Morphisms
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17390v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In generative modeling, standard measure theory adopts the a.e. convention, which legitimately ignores any error component carried by a null-support set: a single null element can hide out-of-domain error inside null support and never be explicitly accounted for. The contribution of this paper is not a new distributional distance, but rather a verifiable structure that writes down which underlying predicate supports a high-level object, when it is invertible, and at which layer the error resides, from which we propose the enumerating posterior-supported prior framework. The framework operates on a three-layer categorical chain Quot->MorTop->Set: the first two layers posit no point elements and take binary-predicate quotient partitions as objects; the replica-index counting measure successively discriminates one-to-many collections into injections, lifting object collection from surjection to a quotient-layer bijection; the mutual exclusion of preimages in the shared measure space is resolved by an invertible MPT. Four results consolidate into Thm. 7: binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects support the set categorical functional along categorical support via measure descent--recovery, enumerating the morphism itself rather than its preimage and object; their multiplicity is normalized through replica-index injection and accounted as an explicitly first-order error. The contribution of this paper is a transformation from nontrivial-input construction -> engineering-computable first-order output: the binary quotient-partition meta-categorical objects, supported via categorical support measure descent--recovery, constitute a substantive nontrivial input---precisely because they lift the out-of-domain error that hid inside null support into a first-order falsifiable coefficient mu_err, a finitely obtainable finite integral first-order error.

entry.title: Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17395v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in weight-space programming (WSP) have demonstrated that large language models (LLMs) can directly inspect and modify neural network weights without conventional gradient-based training. While this capability opens new possibilities for model improvement, it also raises an important security question: Can LLMs exploit weight-space programming to inject backdoors into neural networks? To answer this question, we present an empirical security study of LLM-driven weight-space programming for backdoor injection. Specifically, we investigate whether general-purpose LLMs can directly modify the weights of target models according to natural-language instructions, without accessing task-specific data, performing forward passes, or computing gradients. We evaluate five LLMs as weight editors across three target architectures: an MLP on MNIST, ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, and Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on AG News. Our experiments reveal three key findings. First, LLM-driven weight editing can successfully inject backdoors across different architectures while largely preserving clean performance. Second, successful attacks can require remarkably few parameter modifications, including only six parameters for the MLP and 0.02% of the weights for a fine-tuned Qwen model. Third, editing capabilities vary substantially across LLMs and target architectures: although all five LLMs successfully backdoor the MLP, only GPT-6 Astra succeeds across all three targets. These findings highlight an emerging security risk of weight-space programming and underscore the importance of safeguarding LLM-driven weight editing.

entry.title: WETW: Learning Pair-Specific Weighted Euclidean Distances for Efficient DTW Search [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is the standard distance for similarity search over time series that are misaligned in time, but its cost is quadratic in the series length and lower bounds often prune few candidates, so search over large collections of long series is slow. Learned approximations embed the series to make comparisons cheap, yet compare every pair with the same fixed rule, usually the Euclidean distance, although DTW aligns each pair differently. We observe that, once a pair is aligned, DTW is a Euclidean distance over coordinates selected for that pair. Building on this view, we propose Weighted Euclidean Time Warping (WETW), a learned distance that adapts the comparison of fixed-length embeddings to each pair. A small symmetric network predicts one weight per embedding di- mension and pair without computing an alignment, which halves the error of the best static distance on the same embeddings. The embeddings come from the Weighted Euclidean SEries Encoder (WESEE), whose multi-scale Temporal Feature Extractor keeps the timing information that global pooling removes and raises recall@1 from 0.90 to 0.95, although WETW works with any encoder. We also show that fitting DTW distances is not enough for search, as regression alone misorders the closest neighbours, and that ranking regularization raises recall@1 from 0.79 to 0.95. Our filter-and-verify pipeline, WETW-FV, uses WETW to build a shortlist and exact DTW to check it, so the search is approximate but every returned distance is exact. Over eight datasets, WETW-FV is 11.4x faster than the fastest exact method among the UCR Suite, lower bounds and MESSI-DTW, at a mean recall@10 of 0.93, while the best learned baseline reaches 0.59 at the same speed. On 48K-point series, WETW- FV remains 40x faster than the UCR Suite at a recall@10 of 0.91.

entry.title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17440v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.

entry.title: Racing the Clock: Teaching VLNs Budget-Conditioned Object Search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17442v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A rescue robot entering a building with thirty seconds on the clock should sprint toward the single most promising room; given ten minutes, it should instead explore a broader tour. Yet vision-language-navigation (VLN) models are typically evaluated under a fixed episode limit that the policy never observes, even though time-critical missions require behavior to adapt to the available budget. We study budget-conditioned object search: given a target category and an explicit action budget, an agent must find as many distinct target instances as possible before the budget expires. We investigate how to supervise VLNs for this task by comparing a privileged TSP expert, which plans near-optimal routes using the full map and true target locations, with a room-level Bellman expert that maximizes expected return under partial observability using high-level cross-scene semantic priors. Despite the TSP expert achieving substantially higher expert performance, its demonstrations are less effective for learning exploration: on held-out HM3D scenes, the Bellman-supervised VLN consistently outperforms the TSP-supervised VLN, with the advantage becoming more pronounced at longer budgets. At 2000 steps (500m), the Bellman-supervised VLN finds 71.4% of reachable target instances, compared with 65.5% for the TSP-supervised VLN and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results highlight a distinction between optimal routing and optimal exploration: effective exploration supervision should optimize decisions under partial observability rather than imitate routes that are optimal only once the environment is fully known.

entry.title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.

entry.title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.

entry.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Target-Centric Causal Discovery in Industrial Processes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal discovery promises to find which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality, yield or energy use. Process data with known causes are rare, and in existing benchmarks the difficulty of identifying the causes of a target is either fixed by the recorded data or set for the whole graph. We present a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes. Its generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon of process data, such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target: without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from the direct causes by conditioning on them or by time order. Each component is set independently, so the difficulty can be varied one condition at a time. We evaluate eight methods, from association measures to effect estimation, with an error analysis by the role of the selected candidate; all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions.

entry.title: Binarization as an Attack Surface in Weightless Neural Networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17646v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) are lightweight classifiers that binarize their inputs and learn by storing binary patterns in lookup memories, which makes them attractive for resource-constrained tasks such as intrusion detection. Because a small perturbation that crosses no binarization threshold leaves the binary input unchanged, WNNs may appear naturally robust to adversarial examples; a perturbation that does cross a threshold, however, can still change the prediction. We study this tension in WiSARD, the canonical RAM-based WNN, and in two variants that replace its memories with Bloom filters, Bloom WiSARD and BTHOWeN. A continuous perturbation reaches these classifiers only by crossing an encoding threshold, changing at least one binary tuple, and redirecting a memory query; we formalize this mechanism with a threshold-crossing bound and a response-margin certificate for standard Boolean WiSARD. Controlled MNIST experiments compare linear and data-driven thermometer encodings under model-agnostic sensitivity probes, a score-based Simulated Annealing attack, and surrogate-transfer attacks. Changing only the encoding while keeping each model otherwise fixed shows that encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large decrease in attack success. On the Bot-IoT, CICIDS, and UNSW-NB15 intrusion-detection datasets, adversarial perturbations lead WNN detectors to classify many attacks as normal traffic and to raise false alarms, even when their aggregate accuracy remains high.

entry.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17658v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.

entry.title: Logically Consistent Accurate Forecasts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.

entry.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17753v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.

entry.title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.

entry.title: Multimodal Person Concept Model for Person Identification under Varying Observation Conditions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17802v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content. To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions. The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA). We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination. Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88). We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot. These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. The project page and demonstration video are available at https://okitamisan01.github.io/person_concept/.

entry.title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_\alpha$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.

entry.title: UltraBERT-JEV: Encoder models for System One Applications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study encoder models that pick one of several options in a single forward pass, without generating text. This technical report compares recipes for fine-tuning UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option. The four recipes differ in how an option is scored and how the scores become probabilities; one follows the expert gate of DeepSeek-V3. Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B with the LLM-as-Jev recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%. Scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" instead of "yes" alone gives the larger gain, from 69.7% to 71.3% on the test set and from 57.8% to 59.6% on external benchmarks (56.1% for the decoder). Sigmoid normalisation adds 0.8 test points; a square-root softplus adds none. One request at a time on an NVIDIA A100, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, but uses more peak memory (2.8 against 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head, trained on human-marked evidence and on labels selected with a reward adapted from SelfCite, predicts in the same pass the sentences annotated as support for the answer.

entry.title: From Local Prediction Error to Final Outputs: A Theory of Expert Sharing in Multi-Step Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or computational steps, pooling training information from different contexts. This can reduce local prediction error, but multi-step systems are ultimately evaluated by their final outputs. We study when these local gains survive composition. In specified linear regression models, we derive exact sharing and merging criteria by balancing variance savings against bias from sharing across roles with different target behavior. Under a common fixed linear propagation map, we characterize expected squared final-output risk, retaining error directions and correlations. We construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error. Within this setting, we also identify when orthogonal full pooling with isotropic noise preserves every local improvement at the final output. For general routed computations, we derive conditional end-to-end error bounds that account for distribution shifts, errors in surrounding components, and changes in expert selection. Separately, we show that correct predictions and route labels alone do not establish that individual experts implement the attributed operations. Controlled experiments realize a strict local-to-final risk reversal. In low-data symbolic settings, trained Transformers exhibit statistically supported teacher-forced one-step gains without statistically resolved free-running final-output gains. Separate intervention tests distinguish successful multi-layer actions from single-expert attribution and generalization to unseen transitions. Together, these results distinguish when sharing improves local estimation, when those gains survive to the final output, and what evidence is needed to attribute reusable operations to individual experts.

entry.title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems by Design [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17883v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems solve complex tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, delegating the subtasks to agents, and aggregating the agents' responses using an aggregation rule. Malicious agents can manipulate the final solution by providing malicious responses to their assigned subtasks. In this paper, we first propose response manipulation attacks (ReMA), which iteratively optimize malicious responses to maximize attack effectiveness. Specifically, we formulate untargeted and targeted attacks as optimization problems and develop an approach to approximately solve these problems by iteratively refining malicious responses based on feedback from a surrogate multi-agent system. To defend against such attacks, we further propose SecMAS, a secure aggregation rule that leverages the semantic similarities among agent responses to select the response that is most consistent with a sufficiently large subset of the other responses. We theoretically establish security guarantees for SecMAS against both untargeted and targeted attacks. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that existing aggregation rules are vulnerable to ReMA, whereas SecMAS effectively defends against all evaluated attacks, including adaptive variants of ReMA, while maintaining utility comparable to that of existing aggregation rules.

entry.title: Condensing Law of Security Information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17918v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scaling laws indicate that the generalization error of a large language model (LLM) decreases monotonically with model size once data is sufficient, and the corollary that larger models outperform smaller ones is now widely accepted. We argue that this corollary fails in security: decisions there hinge on anomalous inputs, which are long-tailed (e.g., zero-day attacks) and therefore poorly served by likelihood fitting. Worse still, the capability brought about by scale (e.g., inferring the intended whole from a corrupted part) leads a LLM silently \emph{repair} the anomaly before any downstream security head ever sees it. We formalize this as a tradeoff between two quantities: the cognitive capability $K(W)=I(W;P)$ that a model holds about the world distribution, and the security-information retention $R(W)=\frac{I(Z;S)}{I(A;S)}$ that survives in its intermediate representation. We derive three information-theoretic bounds to connect them: an upper bound on restoration accuracy in terms of $K(W)$, an upper bound on $R(W)$ in terms of the restoration error, and a Fano lower bound on security-task error in terms of $R(W)$. These theorems approximately imply that usable security information is a product of how much security information survives and how well it can be extracted, indicating that optimal usable security information can be achieved at a certain model size. We state this as the \emph{condensing law of security information}: usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and is minimized at a finite $N^{\star}$ rather than decreasing without bound. The experiments on various real-world LLMs validate the condensing law, indicating that there is an optimal model size to solve security issues.

entry.title: MineralExp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Experimental Design in Real-World Mineral Exploration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. Second, open-ended experimental plans resist representation as structured labels, which makes objective scoring difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce MineralExp, a benchmark that reformulates geochemical experimental design as a hypothesis-based experiment selection problem, i.e., a multi-label classification problem. We abstract concrete instrument names and procedural details into a shared taxonomy of 19 experimental types across five mineral-system processes: Source, Transport, Deposition, Modification, and Preservation. This taxonomy yields deterministic multi-label targets while accommodating diverse experimental protocols. Constructed from published ore-deposit literature and verified by domain experts, MineralExp comprises 277 cases and 1,572 reference experimental plans. Given a geological hypothesis and initial context, an LLM agent selects the relevant tasks and generates concrete experimental plans, which are scored by multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. The experimental results show that current agents generally achieve high recall but low precision, tending to propose more experiments than are necessary to test the hypothesis.

entry.title: Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? Drift, Diagnosis and Auditable Intervention on One Shipped Financial Research Agent [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.17939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can you trust a finance agent you did not build? We take the reference agent shipped with the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2, leave it untuned, and ask four questions a leaderboard score does not answer. Is the score stable? Seven identical runs on 18 questions pass between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria, and the bill varies by up to 17%. When the agent fails, who owns the fix? We classify 20 failed trajectories, from three runs of nine held-out questions, by the layer whose owner would remedy them, under a taxonomy frozen in advance: 13 belong to the agent's instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model, none to its data. Can that diagnosis be trusted? Four blind readers from three model families, given only the traces, name the same fault as our LLM analyzer in 94% of cases, the rate at which they agree with one another (93%). Can a change be trusted? An optimization loop reads the traces, makes one targeted change per round and keeps it only if it clears a fixed threshold. Under a cost objective its final configuration costs 0.34x the baseline on the held-out questions (95% CI [0.22, 0.58]) at accuracy within noise. Under an accuracy objective it gains 14 points on the development questions and 1.5 on the held-out ones (CI [-5.3, +7.2]). Judged against the measured run-to-run noise, under a rule written before the test was opened, the first is a real saving and the second is not. This is a case study of one agent and nine test questions, not a general result.

entry.title: RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$: On-Device Reinforcement Learning Runtime [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-device reinforcement learning runs a periodic actor and a learner on one embedded GPU shared with other workloads. Because the learner produces the actor's weights, existing designs stall the actor or let its policy drift. We present RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$, an on-device runtime that makes this coupling a tunable parameter: a refresh bound limits actor releases between refreshes, and a GPU permit with slack-aware admission prioritises the actor and fills spare time with training atop any base scheduler. Under the real refresh cost on two Jetson boards, RL$^{\mathrm{RT}}$ keeps a 16.8 M-parameter policy's deadline misses below 1%, against 85 to 100% without it.

entry.title: T2ST: Data-Efficient Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models via Temporal Data and Knowledge Transfer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
